query: The Co-free FeNiCrMn system was selected to reduce cost while retaining the mechanical performance of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi; prior work reported comparable or better mechanical properties after excluding Co. Research on FeNiCrMn has mainly addressed corrosion, while studies of related high- and medium-entropy alloys examined dynamic responses under tension or compression, different temperatures and strain rates, compositional changes, and the presence of cracks or voids. Those studies established that dynamic properties are sensitive to loading regime and material condition, but their different chemistries and defect states do not identify what governs FeNiCrMn. Under the constraints of retaining the Co-free composition and its strength–ductility balance, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains the dynamic behavior of solidified FeNiCrMn across temperature and strain-rate regimes? Define a controlled study capable of testing the hypothesis, its applicable boundaries, the prior findings that support it, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Under dynamic loading of Co-free, solidified FeNiCrMn at a range of temperatures and strain rates, the dominant plasticity mechanism is governed by partial dislocation slip and cross-slip (with possible fault/twin formation) that sustains high strain hardening and ductility while preserving strength, thereby explaining the alloy’s robust dynamic performance across diverse loading conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: Homogenized, Co-free FeNiCrMn alloy solidified by conventional casting, with a uniform grain size distribution and low initial dislocation density to isolate the effect of subsequent defect evolution.
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to quasi-static and high strain-rate mechanical tests (e.g., compression or tension) spanning 10−3 to 10³ s−1 under temperatures from cryogenic up to 800 °C. Combine these tests with ex situ and in situ microstructural characterization (e.g., TEM, XRD) and complementary crystal-plasticity simulations to track evolving dislocation/twin structures.
generation.conditions: Test samples at multiple strain rates (10−3, 10−1, 10, 102, and 103 s−1) and temperatures (−196 °C, RT, 400 °C, 600 °C, 800 °C) using standard setups (quasi-static compression or tension frames, split-Hopkinson bar) while collecting real-time or postmortem microstructural data.
generation.structural_mediator: Dislocation configurations, stacking fault density, and possible twin boundaries formed during high-rate deformation and elevated-temperature loading.
generation.mechanism: Dislocation slip and dynamic cross-slip, aided by partial dislocations and moderate stacking fault energy, result in enhanced strain hardening and delay plastic instability under both quasi-static and high-strain-rate loading. Elevated temperature promotes additional dislocation climb and recovery, so the dynamic flow stress is set by the competition among dislocation slip, partial dislocation cross-slip, twinning, and thermal activation processes.
generation.predicted_outcome: FeNiCrMn will exhibit increased strain-rate sensitivity and maintain high strength and ductility over the tested temperature range. Electron microscopy will reveal dense dislocation networks and moderate stacking fault/twinning features at lower temperatures and higher strain rates, with localized recovery processes at elevated temperatures. These observations will correlate with crystal-plasticity simulations predicting short-range order and partial dislocation activity during dynamic deformation.
generation.baseline: Measured baseline performance of Co-containing high-entropy alloys (e.g., CoCrFeMnNi variants) in prior dynamic testing studies with known strain-rate and temperature sensitivity.
generation.boundary: Applicable to near-equiatomic Co-free FeNiCrMn in an as-solidified or homogenized state with limited compositional variation. Extreme grain size or large compositional adjustments, and testing regimes significantly beyond the specified strain rates or temperatures, may introduce alternate mechanisms (e.g., brittle phases or dominant twinning) that fall outside this hypothesis.
generation.uncertainty: The relative contribution of twinning versus partial dislocation slip might shift as alloy purity or microstructure changes, and exact threshold conditions for twinning are not precisely known. Some aspects of defect interactions, such as the role of short-range order or local compositional variations, remain to be conclusively identified in FeNiCrMn at high rates and temperatures.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce a series of as-solidified Co-free FeNiCrMn test coupons with varying grain sizes but otherwise identical compositions. Carry out quasi-static (10−3 s−1) and high-rate (≥10³ s−1) compression tests across a wide temperature range (e.g., −196 °C to 800 °C). Perform ex situ and/or in situ electron microscopy and diffraction measurements to quantify changes in dislocation density, presence of stacking faults, and twinning. Correlate observations with predicted dislocation-based plasticity models.
measurements: Stress–strain response at each strain rate and temperature
Strain-rate sensitivity (m-value) derived from flow stress measurements
Dislocation and twin densities via postmortem TEM/EBSD analysis
Localized shear bands or dynamic recrystallization evidence via metallographic characterization
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If significant strength–ductility retention is observed without the predicted rise in partial dislocation and cross-slip activity, or if the alloy’s dynamic response is dominated by an alternative mechanism (e.g., microcracking, phase transformations) rather than partial dislocation mediation, the hypothesis is falsified.

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) are new alloys that contain five or more elements in roughly-equal proportion. We present new experiments and theory on the deformation behavior of HEAs under slow stretching (straining), and observe differences, compared to conventional alloys with fewer elements. For a specific range of temperatures and strain-rates, HEAs deform in a jerky way, with sudden slips that make it difficult to precisely control the deformation. An analytic model explains these slips as avalanches of slipping weak spots and predicts the observed slip statistics, stress-strain curves, and their dependence on temperature, strain-rate, and material composition. The ratio of the weak spots’ healing rate to the strain-rate is the main tuning parameter, reminiscent of the Portevin-LeChatellier effect and time-temperature superposition in polymers. Our model predictions agree with the experimental results. The proposed widely-applicable deformation mechanism is useful for deformation control and alloy design.
